extracted.intended_audience: general readers; writers and thinkers interested in moral, literary, and practical reflection (readers of Montaigne / essayists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing and weighing personal, philosophical, and literary reflections in the Montaigne tradition — emphasis on style, sincerity, and practical worth rather than mere display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombast and empty jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not substitute lofty or technical-sounding words for real substance; grand words that do not correspond to true greatness are merely effects of language, not genuine merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne objects to hearing "architects thunder out their bombast words of pilasters, architraves, and cornices" and likens grammatical jargon (metonymies, metaphors, allegories) to the "babble of my chambermaid." Anti-pattern: using elevated terminology to mask mundane or paltry realities. Aim for words that correspond to what is actually present rather than verbal ornament alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confer grand titles unworthily
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid lavishly bestowing ancient or exalted surnames and honorifics on persons or offices that lack the corresponding authority or excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns against the modern habit of giving the same lofty surnames (e.g., 'Divine' or 'Great') to many who do not match the original holders' merits (Plato, etc.). Example: Italians calling Aretin 'Divine' despite his distance from ancient divinity. Use honors sparingly and appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admire and practise moderation and frugality
rubrics_metrics.description: Parsimony, simplicity of life, and moderate train/possessions are virtues (as exemplified by Attilius Regulus, Cato, Scipio, Homer, Plato, Zeno).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne gives examples (Cato selling his warhorse, Scipio travelling with seven servants) to praise moderation. Implicit scoring: simpler life, modest household, and avoiding ostentation indicate moral seriousness and strength of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine yourself before judging others
rubrics_metrics.description: Spend time inspecting and improving one's own abilities and condition rather than prying into or censoring others' actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne opens the reflection with César's maxim: instead of spending time on others, "employ the time ... in examining our own abilities." Anti-pattern: dwelling on others' faults while neglecting self-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value usefulness over mere novelty or difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not praise things solely because they are rare, novel, or hard to perform; true commendation should be grounded in worth and usefulness as well as difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual maxim: "’Tis a strong evidence of a weak judgment when men approve of things for their being rare and new, or for their difficulty, where worth and usefulness are not conjoined to recommend them." Examples: contrived versifications, feats of dexterity rewarded despite trivial usefulness. When evaluating an accomplishment, ask: does it serve a useful end?

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the dangers of middling (half-formed) learning and pretension
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘middle’ class of thought — neither simple ignorance nor true deep learning — is precarious and often dangerous; both plain naturalness and deep knowledge are preferable to pretended middle competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne contrasts 'Abecedarian ignorance' and 'doctoral ignorance' and condemns the 'mongrels' who have abandoned beginner ignorance but not attained higher understanding ('sitting betwixt two stools'). Anti-pattern: superficial learning that produces arrogance or meddlesomeness rather than wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer natural, popular poesy to contrived middling poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple, artless popular poetry (folk verses, country songs) can possess graces comparable to highly worked poetry; the middling, artificially contrived verse is often worthless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites Gascon villanels and songs from illiterate nations as having 'artless graces.' Implication for writers: value authentic voice and natural expression rather than elaborate but hollow cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scent and perfume should not mask defect; absence of offensive smell is best
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief excellence of the human body, in relation to odor, is to be free from offensive smell; perfumes used to hide defects are suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne quotes Plautus: 'She smells sweetest, who smells not at all.' He criticises excessive exotic perfumes as indications of some natural imperfection being concealed. Prefer simple, natural odors; choose lodgings for clean air. Example anti-pattern: heavy exotic scent used as social camouflage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use perfumes and incense judiciously; simple natural odours please most
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple, natural smells are most pleasing; aromatic usages (including church incense) have purposes (cheer, rouse, purify the senses) but should not substitute for bodily or moral health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes that incense in churches 'was intended to cheer us, and to rouse and purify the senses' and praises simple smells. For sensory design (e.g., hospitality, clothes), favor moderation and natural scent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Lord's Prayer commonly as a primary form
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne favours frequent use of the Lord's Prayer — at table, rising, going to bed, and in many actions — because it comprises all necessary petitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He writes: 'I would that Christians always make use of the Lord’s Prayer... it is most certain that all necessary petitions are comprehended in it.' Practical guideline: keep a simple, comprehensive prayer to hand for ordinary devotion rather than endlessly varied formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure prayers are sincere, prepared, and accompanied by reformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prayer must be offered from a purified soul and followed by visible amendment; invoking God while persisting in vice is hypocritical and often more blameworthy than open vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne insists God’s justice and power are inseparable: '’tis in vain we invoke His power in an unjust cause.' Anti-patterns: habitual, fashion-driven prayer without moral change; mixing devotion with an execrable life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pray with restraint and composed devotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Because it is difficult to compose one’s soul to the calmness required for true prayer, one ought to call upon God less frequently but with full attention and humility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Xenophon and other authorities, Montaigne counsels that frequent casual invocations are 'vain and fruitless.' Prefer fewer, more prepared acts of devotion (sursum corda) rather than constant, thoughtless interjections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat scripture reverently; avoid casual or profane uses
rubrics_metrics.description: The holy scriptures are too serious to be tumbled about as pastime or entertainment; reading should be temperate, premeditated, and performed with veneration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that the Bible 'ought to come from the conscience, and not from the tongue,' and recommends a devout preface ('sursum corda') preparing body and mind. Anti-pattern: using Psalms as lung-exercise or allowing trivialization of sacred texts in kitchens/halls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve interpretation and public exposition of sacred texts to competent persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The dispersion and free exposition of sacred writ into every tongue and into the hands of the unlearned carries danger; qualified judges (learned clergy or properly educated persons) should handle interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne points to historical precedents (Jews, Mohammedans forbidding translation) and warns of the risks of vernacular translations and indiscriminate exposition. Practical rule: limit authoritative teaching and public theological debate to those properly trained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contentious theological disputation that foments schism
rubrics_metrics.description: Contentious dialectic disputes in religion tend to awaken and animate heresies; acquiescence in established formulas often better preserves unity and piety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne records authorities advising against public disputation and gives the anecdote of Andronicus threatening quarrelling divines. Preference: moderation and prudence in theological controversy; avoid inflaming factions for the sake of dialectic victory.
